summary: Defines a binding revocation mechanism for IPv6 mobility, letting one mobility entity ask its peer to end a mobile node's session and free the related resources. It works with Mobile IPv6 and its extensions such as Proxy Mobile IPv6. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: One helper tells another to forget a visitor who is no longer there, so it can throw away the notes.

questions: how to terminate a pmipv6 session
what is binding revocation in mobile ipv6
how does an lma revoke a pmipv6 binding
subtitle: How one mobility node tells its peer to drop a mobile node's binding and free the resources behind it.

tldr.problem: In Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6 a mobility entity sometimes has to end a mobile node's session for administrative reasons or after a handover, but the base protocols give it no way to tell its peer, so state and resources are left behind.
tldr.mechanism: A new Mobility Header message, type 16, carries a Binding Revocation Indication (BRI) from the initiator to its peer, which answers with a Binding Revocation Acknowledgement (BRA). A trigger code gives the reason, and a Global bit lets one message revoke many bindings.
tldr.outcome: Home agents, local mobility anchors and mobile access gateways can clean up bindings quickly and stay in sync. It is protected by the same security association as the binding signaling it revokes.

today: RFC 5846 is a Proposed Standard from June 2010 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the revocation mechanism that works with Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6.

sections.title: Why Bindings Need Revoking
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv6, a mobile node registers a binding with its home agent that links its home address to where it currently is. For administrative reasons it can become necessary to tell the mobile node that its registration has been revoked and that it can no longer receive IP mobility service for its home address. Mobile IPv4 already had a revocation mechanism (RFC 3543), but IPv6 mobility did not.

This document defines one mechanism that works for Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) and its extensions such as Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213). It uses a new Mobility Header (MH) type, 16, and can be used by any two IP mobility entities.

One rule bounds the whole design: a mobility entity may revoke only the mobile node sessions that are currently registered with it.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a helper needs to tell a visitor or another helper that a visit is over. Before this, there was no polite way to do that.

sections.title: How Revocation Works
sections.content:
The node that starts revocation is the initiator. The node that receives the request and answers is the responder. The initiator sends a Binding Revocation Indication (BRI) and the responder replies with a Binding Revocation Acknowledgement (BRA).

  • Mobile IPv6: the home agent sends the BRI to the mobile node. It names the binding by putting the mobile node's home address in a Type 2 routing header. The mobile node replies with a BRA.
  • Multiple care-of addresses: the home agent adds one Binding Identifier (BID) option per binding to revoke. With no BID options, all of the mobile node's bindings are revoked.
  • Proxy Mobile IPv6, LMA to MAG: the local mobility anchor (LMA) sends the BRI to the mobile access gateway (MAG) hosting the binding, naming it with the MN-ID option and, where needed, the Home Network Prefix option.
  • Proxy Mobile IPv6, MAG to LMA: a MAG normally de-registers with a Proxy Binding Update of lifetime zero. To end many sessions at once it sends a BRI with the Global (G) bit set and the Revocation Trigger set to Per-Peer Policy.

In every case the Revocation Trigger field tells the receiver why the revocation is happening.
sections.eli5: One helper says 'please forget this visitor' and says why. The other helper forgets them and replies 'done'. If the first helper wants, it can say 'forget all my visitors' in one go.

sections.title: The Binding Revocation Message
sections.content:
Both messages use Mobility Header type 16. A Binding Revocation Type field says which one it is: 1 for the Indication (BRI) and 2 for the Acknowledgement (BRA). Value 0 is reserved.

The BRI carries a Revocation Trigger, a 16-bit Sequence Number the initiator uses to match the reply (it could be a random number, and implementations MUST ensure there is no collision between outstanding BRIs), and three flag bits:

  • P (Proxy Binding): the revoked bindings are Proxy Mobile IPv6 bindings.
  • V (IPv4 HoA Binding Only): only the IPv4 home address binding is being revoked.
  • G (Global): all per-peer bindings, or multiple bindings sharing a common identifier, are being revoked.

The BRA has a Status field in place of the trigger, copies the sequence number from the BRI, and copies the P, V and G bits back. Mobility options identify which bindings are meant, for example the Home Network Prefix, Mobile Node Identifier, Binding Identifier, IPv4 Home Address and Alternate Care-of Address options. This document defines no new mobility option.

If the messages travel over an IPv4-only network, they are sent with the same UDP encapsulation, ports and IPv4 addresses as the Proxy Binding Update or Binding Update exchange (source and destination swapped for the reply direction).
sections.eli5: It is a short form with a box saying whether it is a request or a reply, a number so the answer can be matched to the question, and a few tick boxes for special cases.

sections.title: Triggers and Status Codes
sections.content:
The Revocation Trigger says what caused the revocation. Per-MN values (below 128) are used when the BRI revokes bindings of one mobile node. Global values (above 128 and below 250) are used when the G bit is set. Values 250 to 255 are for testing only.

The BRA Status field reports the result. Values below 128 mean the BRI was processed successfully, and values of 128 or more mean it was rejected. A partial success is used when some of the named bindings were already released.

New values for all three registries (message type, trigger, status) need Standards Action or IESG Approval.
sections.eli5: The trigger is the reason written on the note, such as 'the visitor moved away'. The status is the answer, either 'done' or a reason why not.

sections.title: Sending, Acknowledging and Retrying
sections.content:
The responder MUST answer a BRI it accepts or rejects with a BRA that copies the sequence number and the P, V and G bits. If the BRI is discarded, for example because its source address is not unicast, no BRA is sent. A node that does not recognize MH type 16 replies with a Binding Error with status 2, as in RFC 3775.

When the initiator gets a BRA whose sequence number matches an outstanding BRI and the status is success, it MUST delete the retransmission timer, the binding or bindings and all associated resources. On any other status it examines the options in the BRA and follows its local policy.

If no BRA arrives before the InitMINDelayBRIs timer expires, the initiator SHOULD retransmit up to BRIMaxRetriesNumber times. Each retry doubles the timeout until it reaches MAX_BRACK_TIMEOUT. After the last retransmission, the initiator SHOULD clean up all resources for the binding anyway.

While waiting, the home agent or LMA sets a revocation-in-progress flag on the binding entry. If a Binding Update arrives in that window, it decides according to the reason for the revocation and local policy.
sections.eli5: Like sending a letter and waiting for a reply. If none comes, you try again, waiting a bit longer each time, and in the end you tidy up your notebook anyway.

sections.title: What Each Role Does
sections.content:
Home agent. It sends the BRI to the mobile node's care-of address with a Type 2 routing header holding the home address. To revoke only the IPv4 home address binding it sets the V bit and includes the IPv4 Home Address option.

Local mobility anchor. It sets the P bit, always includes the MN-ID option and, to pick out one of several bindings, adds Home Network Prefix options. To revoke everything for one MAG it sets G with trigger Per-Peer Policy and no options. To revoke all nodes in a realm it sets G with trigger Revoking Mobility Node Local Policy and an MN-ID option such as @example.com. The LMA MAY delete the tunnel right after sending the first BRI.

It also updates handover behavior from RFC 5213. When the handoff state is unknown, an LMA that supports revocation SHOULD proactively send a BRI with trigger Inter-MAG Handover - Unknown to the previous MAG rather than wait for a de-registration.

Mobile access gateway. On a handover trigger it SHOULD check that the mobile node is no longer attached before accepting; if it is still attached it MUST reject with Revocation Failed - MN is Attached. A MAG can itself send a global BRI to the LMA. If the LMA answers Global Revocation NOT Authorized, the MAG SHOULD NOT retry with the same global request.

Mobile node. It checks that the routing header address is its home address and that it has a matching binding update list entry. It rejects a BRI with the P bit set using Proxy Binding Revocation NOT Supported. Without BID options it treats all of its care-of address bindings as revoked.
sections.eli5: Each helper has its own job. The home base can say 'forget one visitor' or 'forget a whole group'. The doorman checks the visitor has really left before agreeing, and a visitor simply writes back 'ok'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A node may revoke only sessions registered with it. Revocation signaling MUST be protected by the same security association that protects the Binding Update and Binding Acknowledgement signaling. With IPsec, the traffic selectors of the existing policy entry MUST be extended to cover MH type 16, which reuses the existing SAs so they are already up when a revocation must be sent. If IPsec is not used, the mechanism in use MUST protect against the threats named in RFC 3775 and RFC 5213.

A MAG that may create a proxy binding may also revoke it with a lifetime-zero de-registration. A global revocation with trigger Per-Peer Policy hits every session between a MAG and its LMA, so the LMA MUST be locally configurable to authorize it. Policy stores or AAA may be used, but are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Only a helper who looks after a visitor may cross them out, and the note must travel in the same locked envelope as the original sign-up. Crossing out everyone at once needs special permission.
